title: Stellar southpaws: Five Astros lefties combine to shut out Phillies for second straight game - NewsBreak
text: Pitching has propelled two teams meeting at Daikin Park this week to the top of their divisions. No staff rated more wins above replacement than the Phillies’ entering Wednesday, according to FanGraphs. The Astros ’ ranked right behind them. A taut series is proving why. Another pitching duel unfolded Wednesday night and with a similar result. For a second straight game, Astros pitching shut out the visiting Phillies, this time with five left-handers combining for a 2-0 win. “We’ve got a whole stable of (left-handers), and we finally got use them all in a game,” left-handed reliever Bryan King said. “It was pretty cool.” Never in franchise history had the Astros deployed five left-handed pitchers in a game, per MLB.com. The quintet combined to improve Houston’s record to 16-6 in June. It climbed to a season-high 14 games above .500 and finished the night with a 5 ½-game lead in the AL West. Four of the Astros’ eight shutouts this season have occurred this month. They also shutouts in back-to-back games on June 1, against the Rays , and June 3, against the Pirates . The Phillies’ offense awoke Wednesday ranked 10th in the majors in runs per game. Just eight teams had a higher OPS. Seven owned a higher OPS against left-handed pitching. The Phillies have not scored a run in the first 18 innings of this series, all but two of those thrown by left-handers. “That’s what we had available” Wednesday, said Astros manager Joe Espada. “And they were really, really good.” Colton Gordon , the rookie left-hander, gave the Astros five scoreless innings in his eighth major-league start. Steven Okert, Bennett Sousa and King each followed with a scoreless frame. Josh Hader closed the game, converting his 21st save in as many chances this season. Hader matched the Astros’ franchise record for saves without a blown chance to begin a season set by Dave Smith in 1989. “I was telling them, I did (an all-lefties game) a couple times with the Marlins,” Okert said. “We always laughed about it after, ‘Lefty lane came in.’ So now, we got to do it here.” A first-inning RBI single by Isaac Paredes off Phillies starter Zach Wheeler proved enough support. Victor Caratini added a solo home run in the eighth for what proved unneeded insurance. Both teams emerged with a record of 47-33. King, drawing the eighth with setup man Bryan Abreu unavailable, authored an escape act. Brandon Marsh and Trea Turner singled with one out. Kyle Schwarber pulled a chopper to the right side. First baseman Christian Walker gloved it on a leap and looked at third, where Marsh Held. It left Walker with no play, as Schwarber beat him to first, loading the bases with one out. King got ahead 0-2 on Alec Bohm, who battled for eight pitches. Bohm fouled away three pitches before whiffing at a 93.7 mph fastball for strike three. King then induced a ground out from cleanup hitter Nick Castellanos, stranding three runners and preserving a one-run lead. “Just trusting the guys behind me and trusting my stuff, trusting (catcher) Vic (Caratini),” King said. “It’s important in those difficult moments (to remember) it’s not just you, you’ve got everybody else around you.” ASTROS 2, PHILLIES 0 LOB_Philadelphia 7, Houston 6. 2B_Peña (18). HR_Caratini (6), off Strahm. RBIs_Paredes (46), Caratini (18). Runners left in scoring position_Philadelphia 3 (Castellanos 2, Turner); Houston 2 (Peña, C.Walker). RISP_Philadelphia 1 for 5; Houston 1 for 5. GIDP_Peña. DP_Philadelphia 1 (Sosa, Stott, Bohm). Umpires_Home, Marvin Hudson; First, Ryan Blakney; Second, Jacob Metz; Third, Nestor Ceja. T_2:26. A_28,826 (41,000). Gordon navigated the Phillies’ lineup twice in five innings. He scattered four hits, all singles, and benefited from some line drives hit right at Astros infielders. He struck out four and did not walk anyone. Over his last four starts, Gordon has posted a 2.14 ERA in 21 innings. “I think his fastball, he’s been executing it better,” Espada said. “The sweeper today was huge. It got down under on those righties. But I think he gets ahead, he executes, he lets his defense behind them do their job.” Gordon threw 57 of 80 pitches for strikes, relying mostly on his four-seamer and sweeping slider. The Phillies put six balls into play against him with a exit velocity of 98.9 mph or higher. Only one fell for a base hit. The two hardest-hit balls against Gordon yielded lineouts to the left side. Bryson Stott singled to open the fifth inning. Otto Kemp lined a one-out single to left, sending Stott to second and giving the Phillies their first runner in scoring position. Reliever Kaleb Ort started to warm. Gordon froze Marsh on a third-strike sinker, turning the lineup over. Turner arrived for a third look. Gordon threw him four sweepers, each lower than the last. Turner chased the fourth in the dirt for strike three. “Similar to last week, big spot, fifth inning, maybe got one more,” Gordon said. “Either way, got to get that guy out to have a shot at that. … Just telling myself, ‘Hey, biggest at-bat of the day,’ and execute to the best of my ability.” Wheeler had allowed one or zero earned runs in six of his past seven starts. He continued the excellent stretch with six innings of one-run ball. Wheeler worked his 12th quality start in 16 outings and lowered his ERA to 2.55. Only a first-inning hiccup marred his evening. Jeremy Peña, the first hitter Wheeler faced, worked a six-pitch at-bat. The last was a 99 mph four-seam fastball. Peña punched it down the right field line, where it landed fair and one-hopped the wall. Paredes sent a chopper up the middle that kicked off the glove of Turner, the shortstop. Peña scored on Paredes’ single. Wheeler faced 22 more batters and did not allow another run. A walk and a single put two men on base with no outs in the second. Wheeler retired his next three hitters to strand them, starting a stretch of setting down nine in a row. A leadoff walk in the fifth snapped it. Wheeler erased that with a double play. With two on and two out in the sixth, Wheeler struck out Walker on a 97 mph fastball to punctuate his outing. The right-hander allowed four hits, walked three and struck out eight. Their past four games have seen the Astros use four different cleanup hitters. Caratini, the switch-hitter, drew the start there Wednesday against the right-hander Wheeler. Jake Meyers, who hit cleanup Tuesday against left-hander Ranger Suárez, dropped down to seventh. Yainer Diaz and Cam Smith had manned the cleanup spot in Houston’s previous two games. Espada has slotted Smith one spot ahead of Walker in each of the past six games, mostly with those two in the 5-6 spots. But the middle of the lineup has largely been in flux for the last week. Yainer Diaz, who was batting cleanup for much of this month, hit seventh Tuesday and was not in the lineup Wednesday, with Caratini catching and switch-hitter Cooper Hummel at DH. “Trying to get the players in a position where they can have big ABs, matchups that I want to see guys potentially facing the starter or a reliever, juggling some things around,” Espada said pregame. “So I’m trying to do the best I can. And these players understand the position that we are in. But the at-bats have been good. Just trying to find rhythm and consistency is important.” Sign up for Houston Chronicle newsletters here Read the original article on houstonchronicle.com
